summary: 2D screening label: not_2d_applicable. Studio did not run (simulation status: skipped). The gate blocked it because the custom steady experiment has no blocks and no power_w object (it needs 1-128 blocks), and the verdict does not permit a run. The scenario is Thermal management of hotspots in 3-D ICs (W2888620174): a two-die stack with a bonding layer, a 1 mm3 hotspot in each die (6.0e9 and 2.0e9 W/m3), interlayer micro-channel cooling (water, 20 mg/s, 10 C inlet), and a 600 W/mK thermal TSV. The extraction classifies it as custom_2d_steady, so a custom 2D steady run would have no transient trace. It is not a bundled EV6/GCC adaptation, and no pinned Ascend910 or ATPlace sizes, powers, source commit, or generated placement apply, so no illustrative input.flp or one-row input.ptrace was produced. No placement assumption exists because no placement was generated. The final verdict is comparison_valid = false, simulation_allowed = false, and both the input and scientific gates fail. Essential physical mismatches: a true 3D vertical stack, embedded micro-channel convection with coolant temperature rise, a localized TTSV with no 2D analogue, volumetric W/m3 hotspots at fixed 3D positions rather than block watts, and specific boundary conditions (bottom h = 1000 W/m2K at 25 C ambient, adiabatic top and sides). No numerical comparison with the paper's about 70 K micro-channel temperature reduction is made. That value is a line profile at x = 5.0 mm, z = 5.0 mm along y with unstated aggregation, and no Studio output exists to compare against. Qualitatively, the paper reports that micro-channel cooling lowers temperatures substantially and that the TTSV lowers the hotspot temperature further. This cannot be tested here, and no replication is claimed. Independent verification is also missing: code, config, and data checks are unresolved, and the adversarial review and page/asset review did not approve the claims.

The model is a true 3D stack with two active dies, a bonding layer, and a vertical z axis with hotspots at different heights. A 2D single-layer floorplan thermal model cannot represent this vertical heat flow.

Interlayer micro-channel liquid cooling (1.0 x 2.0 mm channel along x, water at 20 mg/s, 10 C inlet) is central to the result. It adds a convective term (eq. 2) and coolant temperature rise that a conduction-only package/heat-sink model does not include.

The thermal TSV (600 W/mK, 1x1x1 mm) between the hotspot and the channel is a key mechanism. It is modeled via an effective conductivity (eq. 3) in a localized 3D volume and has no 2D floorplan analogue.
The heat sources are volumetric 1 mm3 hotspots specified in W/m3 at fixed 3D positions, not block-level watts on a chip floorplan. The workload has no multi-block layout and no power trace.

The boundary conditions are specific: bottom convection h = 1000 W/m2K at 25 C ambient, and adiabatic top and side surfaces. These differ from a typical Studio package stack with a heat sink and spreader.
The paper has no optimizer or controller. The study is a fixed-configuration steady comparison, so there is no placement optimizer or control policy to replicate.

Eq. 1 and eq. 2 include a transient term, but the reported results are temperature profiles for what appears to be a steady state. The paper does not state this explicitly, and no transient or time-series result is given.
The paper does not report reliability, hotspot-lifetime, or electromigration analysis. Only temperature profiles are given.
The packet does not describe the bundled Studio package or material stack, so none can be cited here.
Any Studio run would be a separate illustrative 2D model with its own package and material assumptions and a generated placement. Those coordinates and powers are not paper-derived facts.
Studio temperatures must not be compared numerically to the paper's ~70 K micro-channel reduction or to its profiles, because of the 3D, micro-channel, and TTSV mismatches.
